To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we identified the genes for sulfoligids in the primitive red alga, C. meloreae, and verified the enzymatic function through heterologous expressions.

we have revealed that the system of synthesis of the sulfoquinovose lipid is conserved through evolution from cyanobacteria, to red algae and to green algae, which is compatible for a monophyletic evolution of plastids.
the SQD1 gene for UDP-sulfooquinovose synthesis and the SQD2 gene for sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol formation are present in Cyanidioschzyn merolae.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolutionary history of the thylakoid membrane system.
the evolution of sulfolipids in the red lineage.
the identification of the system for sulfolipids in a red alga, which is one of the most primitive eukaryotic organisms.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the system of SQD1-SQD2-dependent sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol biosynthesis was conserved in a red lineage from cyanobacteria through the endosymbiotic origin of red plastids to green plants.
the SQD1 gene was acquired through horizontal gene transfer in a red lineage and the SQD2 gene was inherited from the common ancestor of plastids.
the system of synthesis of sulfoquinosyl diacylgycerol was already established in the last common ancestor of the cyanobacteria, red algae, green algae, and land plants.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the system of thylakoid membrane construction in C. merolae has evolved in a manner similar to that in cyanobacteria and chloroplasts in green plants, although the red lineage has evolved independently of the other two lineages.
the system of thylakoid lipid synthesis in C. merolae is basically similar to that in the other plastids, but is still primitive as compared with that in the other red algae.

a red lineage is the most primitive red alga, in which a gene system for the synthesis of a thylakoid lipid, sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol, was conserved from a common ancestor of the cyanobacteria and plastids.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the genes for the synthesis of the thylakoid membrane component, sulfoquinovosyldiacylglycerol, were present in the most primitive red alga, C. melorae, which is a member of a red algal lineage that diverged before the emergence of the green lineage, indicating that the genes for sulfoquinovoso-syldiacylglycero-synthesis could have been conscribed from a cyanobacterium to a red alga

the SQD1/SQD2 system is an ancient and conserved mechanism of sulfoquinosyl diacyl glycerol synthesis, and that the system was already established in the common ancestor of the cyanobacteria and plastids.
the system of the synthesis of SQD is conserved in the evolutionary lineage of the red algae.
